PM Controller

Phase 1 — Completion record · schema, auth, admin setup, row-level security

Owner Apex Plumbing and Mechanical Services SC Pilot Paulson Cheek Mechanical Merged PR #1 · 21 September 2026 Status Milestone met

1. The milestone, and how it was proven

"An admin creates a Lead by email, and that Lead sees only his project and cannot read the receipts tables at all."
That is a claim about the database, so it was tested against the database — as the role a phone actually holds (authenticated, with a real signed-in user id), never as the owner, who bypasses every policy. 56 of 56 assertions pass.
AreaTestsWhat is actually asserted
Project isolation9A Lead sees exactly one project. A sub's Lead on another job sees none of the first job's tasks. The same man is Foreman on one job and Super on another.
Material access15Lead reads zero receipts, zero line items, zero categories. A Foreman cannot reach the other Foreman's receipt by id. PM, Assistant PM and Manager read everything.
Sign-off4Lead, Foreman and Assistant PM refused. Super allowed.
History7An Accomplished task cannot be reopened by anyone, the Manager included. task_events cannot be rewritten even by the service role.
Change orders4Assistant PM and Super refused in both directions. PM allowed.
Locked statuses5A seventh status is impossible. rework_count cannot be typed, only derived.
Lead movement4Moves his own task only; cannot create, kick back, or touch another Lead's.
People & cost8A Lead cannot read burdened_rate at all. Nobody can be deleted — deactivation is the only path.

The gate was verified to actually gate. Introducing one deliberate leak — a Foreman able to see another Foreman's receipts — fails five assertions and exits non-zero. A test suite that has never been seen to fail is not evidence of anything.

RefDefectEffect if it had shipped

3. Decision log — how Phase 1 actually went

A record of each request and what came of it. Summarised rather than transcribed, so it stays readable; the commit history and docs/DECISIONS.md carry the detail.

Build it as an Apple app, not a website.
SPEC §9 changed from React PWA to native SwiftUI. Backend untouched — the schema and policies never depended on the client. The three reasons were risks the Phase 0 plan had already flagged: push notifications reaching a Lead with the app closed, camera in one tap, and a close-out surviving no signal.
Name it PM Controller. Separate it from Apex. Tablet first. Add CI.
Renamed throughout. Demo data de-branded. TARGETED_DEVICE_FAMILY "1,2" — one binary, layouts diverging by size class. Three CI jobs added: row-level security, an iPad build, and screenshots of the app running.
Can I see results before paying for a developer account?
Yes — the $99 is only needed to put a build on someone else's device. The real prerequisite was a Mac, and CI covers most of it: GitHub's macOS runners are free on public repositories, so every push now photographs the app on an iPad.
Go as old as iOS 24.
Raised as a factual error: there is no iOS 24, and no 19 through 25. Apple went from 18 straight to 26 in 2025. Read as "the 2024 release" and set to iOS 18 — which also reverted a costly detour to iOS 16 made an hour earlier.
Apex owns the app. Make sure it's in the code.
Reversed the earlier separation. Ownership now asserted in LICENSE, a copyright header on all 17 source files, and NSHumanReadableCopyright so it ships inside the binary.
Use the full legal name. iOS 18 works.
Apex Plumbing and Mechanical Services SC everywhere. Two things a plain replace missed: the name wrapped across a line in LICENSE exactly where the "Apex" shorthand is defined, and the documents were still quoting a bundle identifier that had changed.
apexmech.com is ours. Merge it.
Bundle identifier com.apexmech.pmcontroller confirmed correct. PR #1 merged with a merge commit rather than a squash — three of its six commits record CI failures and their causes, and on a project whose own principle is that the audit trail is the product, discarding that would be the wrong instinct.

Three CI failures, none of them flakes

FailureCause
Incompatible deviceThe simulator picker chose a 2017 iPad Pro that iOS 26.5 will not run. Having a device type and a runtime does not mean they pair. Now reads each runtime's published supportedDeviceTypes.
Generic parameter could not be inferred@EnvironmentObject needs an explicit type where @Environment(Session.self) infers one. Introduced by the iOS 16 conversion that was later reverted.
Missing bundle IDSupplying INFOPLIST_FILE means Xcode synthesises nothing, so CFBundleIdentifier was simply absent and the built app could not be installed.

4. What is verified, and what is not

VerifiedNot verified
• Both migrations apply to a real Postgres 16
• 56/56 policy assertions, run as a signed-in user
• The suite fails loudly when a rule regresses
• The Swift compiles for iPad at the iOS 18 floor
• The app launches and renders every Phase 1 screen 		• The Edge Function has never been deployed
• No migration has run against a live Supabase project

5. Carried into Phase 2

  • App named and locked — PM Controller, com.apexmech.pmcontroller
  • Ownership asserted in the code
  • Deployment floor settled at iOS/iPadOS 18
  • A Mac is available; no Apple Developer Program needed yet
  • CI gates the access rules on every push
  • Create the Supabase project and apply 0001, 0002, then seed
  • Deploy admin-create-user and create the first real Manager
  • Open it in Xcode and run it — the first thing CI cannot do for you
  • Data-ownership terms with PCM in writing before any of its data is entered
  • Confirm which iPads the crews carry — anything below iPadOS 18 is out
  • Burdened rates: real figures, or placeholder multipliers
The one thing to watch. Everything proven so far is proven against a database on a test machine. The first real sign-in, against a real Supabase project, is where Phase 1 stops being a claim. It is a fifteen-minute job and it is worth doing before Phase 2 gets long.

6. Ideas worth keeping

IdeaWhy it came up
Tool disposition flagThe Phase 0 plan had a job-charged vs. returns-to-shop flag on tools that SPEC §6 dropped. It is a real source of quiet job overrun and belongs in Phase 6d.
Screenshots as a review artifactBuilt to work around not having a Mac; worth keeping permanently. Every push produces a visual record of what the app looked like on that commit.
The seed data doubles as preview dataPreview mode mirrors seed.sql, including the man who is Super on one job and Foreman on another. It keeps screenshots honest and makes the per-project role rule visible in every one of them.
The test suite is a sales asset"A Foreman cannot see another Foreman's receipts, and here is the test that proves it" is a stronger claim to a pilot customer than any feature list.
